title: What a 30‑hour S/4 cutover rewrites on your checklist
description: I walk a cutover from the control room to the middleware queue and explain what to check first when a single, short brownfield window is all you get.

stories.headline: Preh completes S/4 conversion with 30-hour window and no Plan B
stories.summary: Preh executed a global S/4 brownfield conversion with a single 30-hour go-live window and no fallback plan. The cutover began on 14 November 2025 and used 102 testers; the actual overrun was 45 minutes versus a one-hour buffer. Post-migration, SAP HANA reporting is reported to be ten times faster and Fiori reduced transaction steps.
stories.why_it_matters: For SAP landscapes with production-critical supply chains, this raises the bar for cutover discipline and rehearsal costs: tight blackout windows mean higher risk if rehearsal, partner coordination or interface validations are incomplete, and may require budget for extended hypercare.

stories.headline: Cole Haan completes global SAP S/4HANA go-live across three regions in 18 months
stories.summary: Cole Haan went live on SAP S/4HANA after an 18-month program that delivered a single global cutover and preserved business continuity, according to Applexus on Nov. 11, 2026. The rollout replaced a 20-year-old AFS environment across North America, Europe and Asia and established a cloud enterprise data platform and AI foundation.
stories.why_it_matters: A single global S/4HANA cutover that retires a 20-year AFS instance reduces integration cost and technical debt while creating a unified data foundation that accelerates analytics and AI investments—impacting near-term migration spend and ongoing maintenance.

take.title: What a 30‑hour S/4 cutover rewrites on your checklist
take.dek: I walk a cutover from the control room to the middleware queue and explain what to check first when a single, short brownfield window is all you get.

sections.heading: A quiet war room, a short clock
sections.body:
It’s 02:00 on go‑live weekend. The screens show job queues and last‑minute transports. People speak in short, specific phrases; no one is rehearsing Plan B because there isn’t time for long debates.

Fact: the conversion began on 14 Nov 2025 [C5]. The planned cutover window was 30 hours [C1], and the operational buffer had been one hour; the team recorded an actual delay of 45 minutes against that buffer [C2]. Preh chose a global big‑bang—every location at once, not a phased rollout [C3]. One hundred and two testers worldwide gradually confirmed the release of their system areas [C4]. The brownfield route was a 1:1 system conversion, after two preparatory projects: New General Ledger and migration to the central SAP Business Partner model [C6].

My judgement: when the clock is that tight the room’s mood changes from “we’ll recover” to “we must not create extra failure modes.” That difference should change checklists and team behaviours immediately.

sections.heading: What I check first in the landscape — in order
sections.body:
Start where the cutover will break things: interfaces. With a 30‑hour single window you cannot rely on slow manual reconciliation. I verify middleware queues, synchronous API timeouts, IDoc retry policies, file ingestion schedules and any handoffs to third‑party systems. Confirm who will flip endpoints and how DNS, TLS certificates and endpoint credentials are rotated.

Next, check the system conversion mechanics. For a 1:1 brownfield conversion you need clear client locks, transport order of operations, database consistency checks, and a tested path to replay the conversion steps. The prior New GL and Business Partner projects mean masters and ledgers are already structurally different—confirm Post‑Conversion reconciliation scripts across finance and master‑data consumers.

Then custom code and interfaces. Line up custom reports, enhancements, user exits and scheduled jobs that touch master data or accounting tables. Prioritise anything that runs in night batches or that assumes old master formats—those are the usual surprises.

Finally, contracts and operational handoffs. With a big‑bang you must know who owns a failing interface: internal teams, an SI, a managed‑service provider or a cloud connector. Ensure SLAs, emergency contacts and escalation ladders are current and reachable during the window.

My judgement: the single‑window, global cutover increases the dependency surface. You cannot treat any interface as low‑risk; every external consumer becomes a potential showstopper.

sections.heading: Teams, tests and the two things to do Monday
sections.body:
Operationalise the testers. One hundred and two testers worldwide signed off on parts of the landscape [C4]. That distributed sign‑off is invaluable—but it only matters if you can map each tester’s scope to your post‑go‑live severity matrix.

Treat the 45‑minute swing against a one‑hour buffer as a warning, not a victory [C2]. A small slippage exposed brittle sequencing and optimistic assumptions about cutover tasks.

My judgement: short, single‑window cutovers with a big‑bang deployment favour repeatability over improvisation. They demand exact checklists, automation of the boring steps, and clearly owned fallbacks (even if the plan is to stay live). The absence of phased rollback options means compensating controls and reconciliation must be near‑instant.

First two things to do on Monday:
1) Produce a cross‑map that links every interface, job and custom object to a named on‑call owner and an explicit rollback or compensation action. Make it visible to every tester and ops person.
2) Automate and rehearse the three highest‑risk interfaces: mock‑fail them, confirm automatic retries and document the manual intervention steps if automation fails.

If you do those two things, you make a tight window survivable; if you don’t, it stays a gamble.

linkedin.share_post:
A 30-hour global cutover, no Plan B.

I walk a cutover from the control room to the middleware queue and explain what an architect must check first when the entire landscape must convert in a single short window. Interfaces, conversion mechanics, custom code and clear operational ownership are the places where a tight, global brownfield cutover will break — and where you can prevent the worst outcomes.

If you run SAP landscapes, the difference between a survivable 30‑hour window and a costly outage is what you verify before the clock starts.

Also in this issue: Cole Haan’s global S/4 go‑live summary, and the Deadline Radar for BW, ECC and PI/PO maintenance.
linkedin.story_post:
A quiet war room at 02:00 changes how you think as an architect.

When a cutover has a 30‑hour single window and no Plan B, your mental model shifts from “we’ll recover” to “we must not create extra failure modes.” That changes priorities: check the interfaces first, lock down conversion mechanics, and map ownership of every failing component before the clock starts.

[YOUR STORY: a time an integration broke at go‑live because a team assumed a consumer would reconcile manually] — if you have a short, single window, that assumption becomes a showstopper. Treat distributed tester sign‑offs as useful only if each tester’s scope maps to a live severity and an on‑call owner.

Practical takeaway: on Monday after such a cutover, produce a cross‑map linking every interface, job and custom object to a named on‑call owner and an explicit rollback or compensation action. Then automate and rehearse the three highest‑risk interfaces.
